# Finding a dentist in England: NHS care, private care and charges

Last updated: 2026-11-27

> This guide covers routine dental care in **England**. Dental charges and arrangements are different in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and we will cover them separately.

After registering with a GP in England, many people assume dentists work the same way: sign up with a nearby practice and it will look after you from then on, and since you have paid the IHS it should be free. In fact, dentists and GPs are two separate systems, and the rules are quite different.

## Dentists are not the same as GPs

With a GP, once you register at a practice, that is where you are seen. Dentists are different.

According to the NHS website, you can contact any NHS dental practice and ask for an appointment. Some practices ask you to fill in a form, which may look like "registering", but this **does not mean you will always be able to get NHS dental care at that practice in future**. Some practices also have waiting lists for new NHS patients. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-contact-any-nhs-dentist)

So don't think of a dental practice like a GP, where "once you are registered, you are sorted". Whether you can get NHS treatment at a particular practice depends on that practice's arrangements.

## How to find a dentist that offers NHS treatment

Usually:

1. use "Find an NHS dentist" on the NHS website to search for practices near you;
2. call or visit the practice and ask whether they are currently taking new NHS patients;
3. if the practice offers both NHS and private treatment, make it clear that you want an NHS appointment.

If several practices tell you they are not taking new NHS patients, the NHS website suggests contacting your local integrated care board (ICB), which arranges local dental services and may be able to tell you where appointments are available. This does not guarantee you will find one straight away; in some areas it really is hard to get an appointment. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-finding-dentist-and-icb)

## The same practice can offer NHS and private treatment

Many practices offer both, so "this is an NHS dentist" does not mean every treatment you have there is on the NHS.

The UK dental regulator, the General Dental Council (GDC), says that any treatment your dentist believes is clinically necessary to achieve and maintain good oral health should be available on the NHS. This refers to clinically necessary treatment; whether other options are covered by the NHS is something you can ask your dentist directly. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-clinically-necessary-on-nhs)

If one course of treatment is partly NHS and partly private, NHSBSA (the organisation that handles NHS charges) explains that:

- if both NHS and private options have been discussed with you, and that part of the treatment cannot be provided under NHS rules, the dentist can mix the two within the same course of treatment;
- in that case the practice **must** give you an FP17DC form or a similar written plan showing which parts are NHS and which are private;
- orthodontics (teeth straightening) cannot be mixed: it must be entirely NHS or entirely private. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-mixing-nhs-and-private)

So when your dentist recommends a treatment, you can ask directly: "Is this NHS or private? How much will it cost?" If it is mixed, remember to ask for the written plan.

## If I have paid the IHS or I am a student, do I still pay for dental care?

Yes. Once you have paid the IHS, you use the NHS on broadly the same terms as people who live here, and people who live here also pay for dental treatment, so you do too. GOV.UK says clearly that after paying the IHS you still need to pay for dental treatment. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ihs-and-students-pay-dental)

Being a student does not make dental care free either. Among the conditions for free treatment below, the only one related to students is "under 19 and in full-time education"; after that age you pay unless you meet another condition. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ihs-and-students-pay-dental)

## Who gets free NHS dental treatment?

Under NHSBSA's rules, the following people get free NHS dental treatment in England:

- people **under 18**;
- people **under 19 and in full-time education**;
- people who **are pregnant or have had a baby in the last 12 months**;
- people receiving certain benefits such as **Pension Credit Guarantee Credit**;
- people with an NHS Low Income Scheme **HC2 certificate**; people with an **HC3** certificate may get partial help, depending on what the certificate says;
- a small number of others in special situations, such as war disablement. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-free-nhs-dental-treatment)

You need to show proof when asked, for example a MAT B1 form or maternity exemption certificate if you are pregnant or have recently given birth, an HC2 or HC3 certificate for low income, or your benefit award letter for Pension Credit. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-free-nhs-dental-treatment)

If you claim free treatment when you are not entitled to it, NHSBSA warns that you may have to pay a penalty charge of up to £100. If you are not sure, check first rather than ticking a box. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-wrong-free-claim-penalty)

## How much does NHS dental treatment cost?

If you do not qualify for free treatment, NHS dental care in England is charged in three bands. From **1 April 2026** the charges are:

- **Band 1: £27.90**. Examination, diagnosis (including X-rays if needed), advice on prevention, and a scale and polish if clinically needed. This is a routine check-up.
- **Band 2: £76.60**. Everything in Band 1, plus treatment such as fillings, root canal treatment, extractions and gum treatment.
- **Band 3: £332.10**. Everything in Bands 1 and 2, plus more complex treatment such as crowns, dentures and bridges.
- **Urgent treatment: £27.90**. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-nhs-dental-bands)

Each band includes everything in the band below it. Some things are free, such as removing stitches, stopping bleeding after an extraction, and repairing dentures that can be fixed. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-nhs-dental-bands)

These are standard NHS charges and only apply to NHS treatment.

## Roughly how much does private dental treatment cost?

There is no national price for private treatment. The GDC says there are no set limits on what practices can charge for private treatment, and practices should clearly display a simple price list in reception or the waiting area. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-private-fees-no-cap)

To give you a rough idea, below are prices published by a few practices in England that we checked in October 2026. These are only examples, not official prices, and they do not represent an average; "from" means the lowest price, and more complex cases cost more:

- Whites Dental in London: examination £65, white fillings from £160, crowns from £800;
- SpaDental Glastonbury in Somerset (non-member prices): routine examination £82.50, white fillings from £184.20, crowns from £1,037.80;
- Collegiate Dental in Manchester: check-ups from £83, fillings from £167;
- standard prices published by the mydentist chain for England and Wales: white fillings from £174, root canal treatment from £436, crowns £826. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-private-fee-examples)

Prices vary widely between practices, cities and how complex the treatment is. Before deciding on private treatment, it is best to get a written treatment plan and quote, ask what steps are included and whether there will be any extra costs later, and then decide.

## Changing dentist

As explained above, NHS dentists do not use fixed registration like GPs, so if you want to change, you can simply contact other practices and ask whether they are taking NHS patients. Whether you can get an appointment depends on that practice.

## What if I have bad toothache?

This guide is about routine dental care. Sudden severe toothache or a swollen face is a different route: contact the dental practice you usually go to, or if you don't have one, call NHS 111, which will tell you what to do. A GP cannot treat your teeth. How to judge the situation and when to go to A&E are covered in our separate guide on sudden toothache. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-toothache-route)

## Official sources

- NHS Business Services Authority (NHSBSA) — *Current NHS dental charges* (FAQ KA-02003) — https://faq.nhsbsa.nhs.uk/knowledgebase/article/KA-02003
- NHS Business Services Authority (NHSBSA) — *Free NHS dental treatment* — https://nhsbsa.nhs.uk/help-nhs-dental-costs/free-nhs-dental-treatment
- NHS Business Services Authority (NHSBSA) — *Mixing NHS and private dental treatment* (FAQ KA-02022) — https://faq.nhsbsa.nhs.uk/knowledgebase/article/KA-02022/en-us
- General Dental Council — *Dental costs* — https://www.gdc-uk.org/standards-guidance/information-for-patients-public/dental-costs
- GOV.UK — *Pay for UK healthcare as part of your immigration application* — https://www.gov.uk/healthcare-immigration-application
